subtopic: Hyperglycaemic emergency: HHS rather than DKA
stem:
An 82-year-old woman from a nursing home in Toowoomba, Qld, is brought in after three days of increasing drowsiness. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. She is drowsy but rousable. Pulse 112/min, BP 98/60 mmHg, dry mucous membranes.

Investigations:
- Blood glucose 46 mmol/L
- Sodium 149 mmol/L (135–145)
- Calculated serum osmolality 352 mOsm/kg (275–295)
- Capillary ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate) 0.6 mmol/L
- Venous pH 7.34, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L
lead_in: Which one of the following best explains these findings?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: Mixed DKA and HHS
options.D: Hypernatraemic dehydration without a diabetic emergency
options.E: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

explanation_correct: The JBDS guideline describes HHS as hypovolaemia with osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg and marked hyperglycaemia (above 30 mmol/L), without significant ketonaemia or acidosis. She meets all of these: osmolality 352, glucose 46, ketones 0.6, pH 7.34, bicarbonate 21. The distinction affects treatment. In HHS, IV fluids come first and insulin is held until glucose stops falling, unless there is significant ketonaemia.

option_explanations.A: DKA needs significant ketonaemia (≥3 mmol/L) with acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15). She has neither.
option_explanations.B: A mixed picture needs both hyperosmolality and significant ketonaemia or acidosis. Her ketones and pH are near normal.
option_explanations.C: Her pH and bicarbonate are near normal, so she has no significant acidosis.
option_explanations.D: A glucose of 46 mmol/L with osmolality of 352 is a hyperglycaemic emergency, not simple dehydration.

key_learning_point: HHS: osmolality above 320, glucose above 30 mmol/L, hypovolaemia, and no significant ketonaemia or acidosis.

references.name: Joint British Diabetes Societies. The Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (Feb 2022)

subtopic: Sulfonylurea overdose: octreotide for recurrent hypoglycaemia
stem: A 46-year-old woman presents to a Brisbane emergency department four hours after taking an unknown number of her mother's gliclazide modified-release tablets. On arrival her blood glucose was 2.1 mmol/L and she was given 50 mL of 50% glucose IV. A 10% glucose infusion was then started. Over the next two hours her glucose falls to 3.2 mmol/L twice despite the infusion. She is alert and her observations are otherwise normal.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.A: Repeated 50% glucose boluses as needed
options.B: Octreotide
options.D: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV
options.E: Activated charcoal 50 g orally

explanation_correct: Sulfonylureas trigger ongoing insulin release, and repeated glucose boluses make it worse by stimulating more secretion. Octreotide suppresses insulin release. Queensland Poisons Information Centre antidote guidance recommends octreotide for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia (BSL <4.0 mmol/L) after the first glucose correction.

option_explanations.A: Repeated boluses stimulate further insulin release from the sulfonylurea-primed pancreas and cause rebound hypoglycaemia.
option_explanations.C: Glucagon has a brief effect, relies on liver glycogen and also stimulates insulin release. It is not the treatment for sulfonylurea toxicity.
option_explanations.D: Corticosteroids have no role in treating sulfonylurea-induced hyperinsulinaemia.
option_explanations.E: Charcoal may be considered early in a cooperative patient, but it does not treat the hypoglycaemia that is already happening.

key_learning_point: Recurrent hypoglycaemia after a sulfonylurea overdose needs octreotide, which blocks insulin release, rather than more glucose boluses.

subtopic: Chronic hepatitis C: hepatitis B serology before DAA treatment
stem: A 38-year-old man sees his GP in Geelong, Vic. He injected drugs 10 years ago. HCV antibody is positive and HCV RNA is detectable. He has never been treated, and the GP plans to prescribe sofosbuvir/velpatasvir. His liver function tests are mildly raised and full blood count is normal. He takes no medicines. He has never had hepatitis B or HIV testing.
lead_in: Which one of the following tests is most important to request before starting treatment?

options.A: Liver biopsy to stage fibrosis
options.B: Serum alpha-fetoprotein and liver ultrasound
options.D: Hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs)
options.E: Hepatitis E IgG and IgM serology

explanation_correct: The Australian HCV guidelines' pre-treatment assessment includes testing for HBV coinfection (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HIV and HAV serology, FBE, LFTs, eGFR, INR, a fibrosis assessment (such as APRI), and a review of drug interactions. The guidelines have a separate section on treating HCV with HBV coinfection, because coinfection changes how treatment is monitored and managed.

option_explanations.A: Fibrosis is assessed non-invasively (APRI, FIB-4 or elastography). Biopsy is not needed.
option_explanations.B: AFP is used for HCC surveillance in cirrhosis, not as a pre-treatment test for everyone.
option_explanations.C: Genotype is optional (it 'may be considered') when a pan-genotypic regimen is used.
option_explanations.E: Hepatitis E serology is not part of the pre-treatment assessment.

key_learning_point: Before HCV DAA treatment, test for HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs) and HIV, assess fibrosis, and check for drug interactions.

subtopic: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia: AChR antibody
stem: A 34-year-old woman in Hobart, Tas, has had drooping of her left eyelid and double vision for six weeks. Both are worse in the evenings and after reading. On examination she has left ptosis that worsens with sustained upgaze for 60 seconds and variable diplopia. Pupils are equal and reactive. Limb power, reflexes and sensation are normal.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?

options.A: MRI brain with gadolinium
options.B: Lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands
options.D: Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies
options.E: Nerve conduction studies with F-waves

explanation_correct: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal pupils suggest myasthenia gravis. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies are the first diagnostic test. They are found in most generalised cases and about half of purely ocular cases. Anti-MuSK antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG come next if AChR antibodies are negative. CT of the chest is then needed to look for a thymoma.

option_explanations.A: MRI is used if there are signs of a brainstem lesion or if pupils are involved. It does not confirm myasthenia.
option_explanations.B: CSF findings are normal in myasthenia. This test is for demyelination.
option_explanations.C: CK is normal in myasthenia. It is raised in myopathies.
option_explanations.E: Standard NCS are normal in myasthenia. Repetitive stimulation, not F-waves, is the relevant neurophysiology test.

key_learning_point: Fatigable ptosis or diplopia with spared pupils points to myasthenia gravis. Test serum AChR antibodies first.

references.name: Healthed (Australian GP education). Clinical Conversations: Myasthenia gravis – a practical approach for GPs, part two

subtopic: Optic neuritis: MRI predicts MS risk
stem: A 27-year-old woman in Adelaide, SA, has had pain on moving her right eye and blurred central vision for four days. Visual acuity is 6/36 right and 6/6 left. She has a right relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced red colour saturation, and the right optic disc looks normal. Two years ago she had three weeks of numbness from the waist down that resolved without treatment.
lead_in: Which one of the following findings would most strongly support a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?

options.A: A normal optic disc on fundoscopy
options.B: Periventricular and juxtacortical T2 lesions on MRI brain, with one lesion enhancing with gadolinium
options.C: A visual evoked potential with prolonged latency in the right eye
options.D: Positive serum aquaporin-4 antibodies
options.E: Raised ESR of 45 mm/h

explanation_correct: She has typical demyelinating optic neuritis after an earlier episode suggestive of a spinal cord lesion. MS is diagnosed by showing dissemination in space and time (McDonald criteria). Lesions in typical locations (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial or spinal) show dissemination in space. Having enhancing and non-enhancing lesions at the same time shows dissemination in time.

option_explanations.A: Retrobulbar neuritis usually shows a normal disc. This fits optic neuritis but says nothing about MS.
option_explanations.C: This confirms demyelination of the affected nerve that is already clinically apparent, but adds no evidence of spread elsewhere.
option_explanations.D: AQP4 antibodies indicate neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which is a different condition from MS.
option_explanations.E: ESR is non-specific. A raised value would make you think of giant cell arteritis or another inflammatory cause, not MS.

key_learning_point: In optic neuritis, MRI brain lesions in typical MS locations, with both enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, satisfy dissemination in space and time.

references.name: Thompson AJ et al. Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria. Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-73 (full-text copy read)

subtopic: Drug-induced parkinsonism from metoclopramide
stem: A 78-year-old woman in Bendigo, Vic, is seen by her GP because her daughter has noticed she is slower and shuffling. Over the past two months she has developed a symmetrical resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity in both arms. She has gastroparesis and started regular metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily three months ago. She has no other new medicines.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

options.A: Idiopathic Parkinson disease
options.B: Essential tremor
options.D: Dopamine D2 receptor blockade by metoclopramide
options.E: Progressive supranuclear palsy

explanation_correct: Symmetrical parkinsonism starting soon after a dopamine antagonist is typical of drug-induced parkinsonism. Metoclopramide is a common cause, especially in older women. The treatment is to stop the drug. Recovery may take weeks to months.

option_explanations.A: Idiopathic Parkinson disease is usually asymmetrical at onset. A symmetrical onset that follows a dopamine blocker points to the drug.
option_explanations.B: Essential tremor is a postural or action tremor without bradykinesia or rigidity.
option_explanations.C: NPH causes gait apraxia with urinary incontinence and cognitive decline, not a resting tremor with arm rigidity.
option_explanations.E: PSP causes early falls and a vertical gaze palsy, and it does not follow a new drug.

key_learning_point: Symmetrical parkinsonism after starting metoclopramide is drug-induced (D2 blockade). Stop the drug.

references.name: Australian Prescriber. Drug-induced movement disorders

subtopic: COPD exacerbation: target SpO2 88–92%
stem:
A 69-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 32% predicted) is brought by ambulance to a hospital in Launceston, Tas, with three days of increasing breathlessness and purulent sputum. Paramedics started oxygen at 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask. His SpO2 is now 99%, respiratory rate 24/min and he is drowsy.

Venous blood gas: pH 7.29, pCO2 68 mmHg.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate change to his oxygen therapy?

options.A: Continue 15 L/min because he is hypoxic from the exacerbation
options.B: Stop oxygen completely
options.C: Change to nasal prongs at 6 L/min aiming for SpO2 above 94%
options.D: Give IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis
options.E: Titrate oxygen by Venturi mask to a target SpO2 of 88–92%

explanation_correct: High-flow oxygen in COPD can worsen hypercapnia (through V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect). His drowsiness and acidosis point to this. COPD-X recommends controlled oxygen titrated to SpO2 88–92%, with blood gases repeated. He will also need non-invasive ventilation if the acidosis persists.

option_explanations.A: An SpO2 of 99% is well above target, and the high-flow oxygen is contributing to his hypercapnic acidosis.
option_explanations.B: Stopping oxygen abruptly can cause dangerous rebound hypoxaemia. Titrate to target instead.
option_explanations.C: This target is too high for a COPD patient with hypercapnia.
option_explanations.D: Respiratory acidosis is managed by controlling oxygen and supporting ventilation, not with bicarbonate.

key_learning_point: In a COPD exacerbation, titrate oxygen to SpO2 88–92%. Over-oxygenation worsens hypercapnic acidosis.

subtopic: Pharyngeal gonorrhoea: timing of test of cure
stem: A 26-year-old man who has sex with men attends a sexual health clinic in Darlinghurst, NSW. His routine screen showed a positive pharyngeal NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, with negative urine and anorectal NAATs. No culture swab was taken. He is treated today with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM and azithromycin 2 g orally. He asks what follow-up testing he needs.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate follow-up test?

options.A: Repeat pharyngeal NAAT 2 days after treatment
options.B: No further testing because the regimen is highly effective
options.C: Repeat pharyngeal NAAT 2 weeks after treatment as a test of cure
options.D: Serum gonococcal antibody titre
options.E: Repeat urine NAAT only at 3 months

explanation_correct: The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend a test of cure by NAAT at each infected site 2 weeks after treatment is completed. This is especially important for pharyngeal infection, when no culture was collected before treatment, or when resistance is suspected. If the test of cure is positive, seek specialist advice.

option_explanations.A: NAAT can detect residual non-viable DNA for days after treatment. Testing at 2 days risks a false-positive result.
option_explanations.B: A test of cure is still recommended for pharyngeal gonorrhoea.
option_explanations.D: There is no useful serological test for gonorrhoea.
option_explanations.E: Retesting at 3 months is for reinfection. It does not replace a site-specific test of cure.

key_learning_point: After treating pharyngeal gonorrhoea, do a test of cure by NAAT 2 weeks after treatment.

references.name: Australian STI Management Guidelines. Gonorrhoea

subtopic: Torsades de pointes: IV magnesium
stem:
A 64-year-old woman on a medical ward in Darwin, NT, is being treated for community-acquired pneumonia with azithromycin. She also takes citalopram and has had diarrhoea for two days. Her monitor shows recurrent runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting QRS axis that end on their own. Between episodes she is alert, BP 122/74 mmHg, and her ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 590 ms.

Serum potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2).
lead_in: In addition to stopping QT-prolonging drugs and replacing potassium, which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.A: Magnesium sulfate 5 mmol intravenously over 10 minutes
options.B: Intravenous amiodarone
options.D: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion
options.E: Oral metoprolol

explanation_correct: This is torsades de pointes from an acquired long QT (macrolide, SSRI, hypokalaemia, possibly hypomagnesaemia from diarrhoea). ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 says to treat immediately: stop all QT-prolonging drugs, correct electrolytes (especially potassium), and give IV magnesium 5 mmol over 10 minutes. This can be repeated once and followed by 20 mmol over 4 hours. Pacing or isoprenaline may be needed to prevent relapse. Amiodarone should be avoided because it can make things worse. Synchronised cardioversion is for adverse signs.

option_explanations.B: ANZCOR states amiodarone should be avoided in torsades because it can worsen the situation.
option_explanations.C: Sotalol is a class III drug that prolongs the QT interval further and can itself cause torsades; it is contraindicated here.
option_explanations.D: ANZCOR reserves cardioversion for adverse signs. She is alert and normotensive between self-terminating runs.
option_explanations.E: Beta-blockade is not the acute treatment for acquired torsades.

key_learning_point: Torsades: stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct potassium, give IV magnesium 5 mmol over 10 minutes, and avoid amiodarone.

references.name: ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias

subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome in an adult: anti-PLA2R and membranous nephropathy
stem:
A 55-year-old man in Ballarat, Vic, has had swelling of his legs for two months. He has no diabetes and takes no regular medicines. BP 136/84 mmHg, pitting oedema to the knees.

Investigations:
- Urine albumin:creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol
- Serum albumin 22 g/L (35–50)
- Creatinine 88 µmol/L (60–110)
- Total cholesterol 9.1 mmol/L
- Urine microscopy: no red cell casts
- Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV serology negative; ANA negative; complement normal
- Serum anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibodies: strongly positive
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Primary membranous nephropathy
options.B: Minimal change disease
options.D: IgA nephropathy
options.E: Lupus nephritis

explanation_correct: Anti-PLA2R antibodies are highly specific for primary membranous nephropathy, the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in middle-aged and older white adults. KDIGO 2021 says a kidney biopsy is no longer required to confirm membranous nephropathy in patients with nephrotic syndrome and a positive anti-PLA2R test. Secondary causes (malignancy, infection, lupus, drugs) should still be looked for.

option_explanations.B: Minimal change is the main cause in children and can occur in adults, but it is not associated with PLA2R antibodies.
option_explanations.C: FSGS is a common cause in adults, but PLA2R antibodies are negative.
option_explanations.D: IgA nephropathy usually causes haematuria, often after an upper respiratory infection, and rarely causes heavy nephrotic syndrome.
option_explanations.E: ANA is negative and complement is normal, which argues against lupus.

key_learning_point: Strongly positive anti-PLA2R antibodies in adult nephrotic syndrome point to primary membranous nephropathy.

references.name: KDIGO 2021 Glomerular Diseases Guideline – Executive summary (Kidney Int)

subtopic: Mildly raised prolactin without symptoms: check for macroprolactin
stem:
A 34-year-old woman in Cairns, Qld, had a prolactin level included in tests for fatigue. Her periods are regular, she has no galactorrhoea or headaches, and a pregnancy test is negative. She takes no medicines.

Investigations:
- Prolactin 1,150 mIU/L (<500), unchanged on repeat
- TSH normal
- eGFR normal
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: MRI of the pituitary with gadolinium
options.B: Formal visual field testing (perimetry)
options.D: Start cabergoline and recheck prolactin
options.E: Insulin tolerance test of pituitary reserve

explanation_correct: Australian Prescriber notes that at least 10% of hyperprolactinaemia is due to macroprolactin, a complex that is cleared slowly from the circulation and is largely biologically inactive. That is why most people with macroprolactinaemia have no symptoms. In a woman with confirmed mild hyperprolactinaemia, no symptoms, and pregnancy, drugs, hypothyroidism and kidney disease excluded, macroprolactin screening comes before pituitary imaging.

option_explanations.A: Imaging is used for true (monomeric) hyperprolactinaemia. Doing it first risks finding an incidental lesion.
option_explanations.B: Visual fields are tested when a macroadenoma is suspected. She has no symptoms and her prolactin is only mildly raised.
option_explanations.D: Treatment is not indicated until true hyperprolactinaemia from a cause that needs treatment is confirmed.
option_explanations.E: Dynamic tests of pituitary reserve are for suspected hypopituitarism; she has no features of it, and the first question is whether the prolactin is biologically active at all.

key_learning_point: Mild hyperprolactinaemia without symptoms: check for macroprolactin before pituitary MRI.

references.name: Australian Prescriber. Hyperprolactinaemia (full text via PubMed Central, PMC5768604)

subtopic: Long-term metformin: vitamin B12 deficiency
stem:
A 72-year-old man in Orange, NSW, has had tingling in both feet for four months and feels more tired. He has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years treated with metformin 1 g twice daily. His HbA1c is 6.9%. He eats a mixed diet. There is reduced vibration sense at the toes.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130–180)
- MCV 104 fL (80–100)
- Serum B12 105 pmol/L (>150)
- Folate normal
- TSH normal
- Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies negative
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his macrocytosis?

options.A: Pernicious anaemia
options.B: Dietary B12 deficiency
options.D: Metformin-associated vitamin B12 malabsorption
options.E: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy

explanation_correct: Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption in the ileum. B12 deficiency can cause macrocytic anaemia and a neuropathy that can be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy. B12 should be checked periodically in long-term metformin users, especially those with anaemia or neuropathy. He needs B12 replacement, and metformin can usually continue.

option_explanations.A: Pernicious anaemia is the commonest cause of severe B12 deficiency, but his intrinsic factor antibodies are negative and he has 12 years of high-dose metformin, the best explanation here.
option_explanations.B: He eats a mixed diet, so dietary deficiency is unlikely.
option_explanations.C: Hypothyroidism can cause a mild macrocytosis, but his TSH is normal and it would not explain a B12 of 105 pmol/L.
option_explanations.E: Neuropathy alone does not explain macrocytic anaemia with a low B12.

key_learning_point: Long-term metformin can cause B12 deficiency, with macrocytosis and neuropathy. Check B12 in these patients.

references.name: Australian Prescriber. Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment

subtopic: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: Hutchinson sign
stem: A 70-year-old woman presents to her GP in Mackay, Qld, with two days of burning pain over her right forehead followed by a vesicular rash in the distribution of the right ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Valaciclovir is started.
lead_in: Which one of the following examination findings most strongly predicts eye involvement and the need for urgent ophthalmology review?

options.A: Vesicles on the upper eyelid
options.B: Vesicles on the tip of the nose
options.D: Rash extending to the scalp vertex
options.E: Pain over the forehead before the rash

explanation_correct: Hutchinson sign is vesicles on the tip, side or root of the nose. It means the nasociliary branch of V1 is involved, and that branch also supplies the cornea. It strongly predicts ocular herpes zoster (keratitis or uveitis). Any patient with HZO, and especially Hutchinson sign, red eye or reduced vision, needs prompt ophthalmology assessment with a slit lamp.

option_explanations.A: Eyelid involvement is common in HZO but predicts eye involvement less strongly than nasal tip lesions.
option_explanations.C: Preauricular nodes may enlarge with any eyelid or conjunctival inflammation; they are non-specific and do not predict corneal or uveal involvement.
option_explanations.D: The vertex lies in the V1 dermatome via the supraorbital and supratrochlear branches, which do not supply the globe.
option_explanations.E: Prodromal pain is typical of shingles and does not predict eye involvement.

key_learning_point: Hutchinson sign (vesicles on the nasal tip) means nasociliary involvement. Expect ocular zoster and refer urgently.

references.name: CMAJ. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (Practice)

subtopic: Mycoplasma genitalium: macrolide-resistance testing to guide therapy
stem: A 29-year-old man in Adelaide, SA, has had dysuria and a mild urethral discharge for three weeks. Urine NAATs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea are negative. His symptoms continued after 7 days of doxycycline. A first-pass urine NAAT is now positive for Mycoplasma genitalium.
lead_in: Which one of the following additional laboratory results will most directly determine his antibiotic regimen?

options.A: Urethral swab culture for M. genitalium with antibiotic sensitivities
options.B: Gram stain of the urethral discharge for polymorphs
options.C: Macrolide-resistance mutation testing on the positive specimen
options.D: Syphilis serology and HIV antigen/antibody testing
options.E: Repeat chlamydia NAAT on a first-pass urine

explanation_correct: The Australian STI Management Guidelines report that macrolide resistance in M. genitalium is above 60% in Australia and above 80% in men who have sex with men. They recommend resistance-guided therapy. After doxycycline, susceptible infection is treated with azithromycin (1 g, then 500 mg daily for 3 days), and macrolide-resistant infection with moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days. NAATs that detect macrolide-resistance mutations make this choice possible.

option_explanations.A: M. genitalium grows very poorly in culture, which is not used clinically.
option_explanations.B: A Gram stain may show urethritis but cannot guide M. genitalium treatment.
option_explanations.D: Syphilis serology is part of STI screening but does not affect the M. genitalium regimen.
option_explanations.E: Chlamydia was already negative, and repeating the test will not change the regimen.

key_learning_point: For M. genitalium, use resistance-guided therapy: doxycycline, then azithromycin if macrolide-susceptible or moxifloxacin if resistant.

references.name: Australian STI Management Guidelines. Mycoplasma genitalium

subtopic: Severe aortic stenosis: exertional syncope as symptom trigger
stem: A 76-year-old man in Wagga Wagga, NSW, collapsed while walking up a hill and recovered within a minute. He has had increasing breathlessness on exertion for three months. He has an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, with a soft second heart sound. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy.
lead_in: Which one of the following echocardiographic findings best indicates that he needs aortic valve intervention?

options.A: Peak velocity 2.8 m/s with a mean gradient of 18 mmHg
options.B: Aortic valve sclerosis without restricted leaflet opening
options.D: Peak aortic jet velocity 4.4 m/s with a mean gradient of 46 mmHg
options.E: Left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%

explanation_correct: Severe aortic stenosis is defined by a peak velocity of at least 4 m/s, a mean gradient of at least 40 mmHg or a valve area under 1.0 cm². When a patient with severe AS has symptoms (exertional syncope, angina or breathlessness), surgical or transcatheter valve replacement is indicated, because prognosis is poor without it.

option_explanations.A: A peak velocity below 3 m/s and mean gradient below 20 mmHg are mild aortic stenosis; they do not meet the severe threshold for valve intervention and would not explain exertional syncope.
option_explanations.B: Sclerosis is not stenosis and does not need intervention.
option_explanations.C: This does not explain his symptoms or carry the same indication.
option_explanations.E: A preserved ejection fraction does not by itself indicate the need for intervention.

key_learning_point: Severe AS (≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, AVA <1.0 cm²) with symptoms is an indication for valve replacement.

subtopic: Suspected acute pancreatitis: serum lipase as the preferred test
stem: A 48-year-old man presents to an emergency department in Bunbury, WA, with 10 hours of severe constant epigastric pain radiating to his back and vomiting. He drinks about 8 standard drinks a day. Pulse 104/min, BP 128/80 mmHg, temperature 37.6°C. He has epigastric tenderness without peritonism.
lead_in: Which one of the following blood tests is most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?

options.A: Serum lipase
options.B: Serum amylase
options.D: Serum calcium
options.E: Serum triglycerides

explanation_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when at least two of three criteria are met: characteristic pain, raised amylase or lipase (at least three times the upper limit of normal), and imaging findings. Australian Prescriber states lipase is now the preferred test. It is more sensitive, particularly in alcohol-related pancreatitis, and stays raised longer, so the diagnostic window is wider.

option_explanations.B: Amylase is less sensitive, especially in alcohol-related disease, and returns to normal sooner.
option_explanations.C: CRP helps assess severity at about 48 hours but does not make the diagnosis.
option_explanations.D: Calcium is part of severity assessment and looking for a cause, not diagnosis.
option_explanations.E: Triglycerides help find a cause. They do not confirm pancreatitis.

key_learning_point: Lipase (≥3 × ULN) is the preferred blood test for diagnosing acute pancreatitis.

subtopic: Raised PSA: mpMRI before biopsy
stem: A 61-year-old man in Toowong, Qld, has a PSA of 6.8 µg/L on testing he chose after discussion with his GP. A repeat PSA six weeks later is 7.1 µg/L. Digital rectal examination finds a smooth, mildly enlarged prostate. He has no urinary symptoms and a urine dipstick is normal. He is referred to a urologist.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Multiparametric MRI of the prostate
options.B: Systematic 12-core transrectal biopsy
options.D: Nuclear medicine bone scan
options.E: Repeat PSA in 12 months

explanation_correct: The 2026 Australian guidelines for early detection of prostate cancer recommend multiparametric MRI as the next test after a confirmed raised PSA, before any biopsy. Biopsy is recommended for PI-RADS 4–5, or for PI-RADS 3 with a PSA density of 0.15 or more. This approach avoids unnecessary biopsies and finds fewer insignificant cancers.

option_explanations.B: Going straight to systematic biopsy without MRI is no longer recommended.
option_explanations.C: CT has no role in detecting cancer within the prostate.
option_explanations.D: Staging scans are only done after cancer is diagnosed and its risk is defined.
option_explanations.E: The PSA is confirmed raised and he needs further assessment now.

key_learning_point: After a confirmed raised PSA, the next test is mpMRI. Biopsy depends on the PI-RADS score and PSA density.

subtopic: Stable blunt splenic injury: CT with arterial and portal venous phases
stem: A 24-year-old man was tackled during a rugby league match in Penrith, NSW, and now has left upper quadrant pain and left shoulder-tip pain. At a major trauma centre, after 1 L of crystalloid, his pulse is 88/min and BP 128/76 mmHg, stable over an hour. He has left upper quadrant tenderness without peritonism. FAST shows a small amount of free fluid in the left upper quadrant.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: CT abdomen with IV contrast in arterial and portal venous phases
options.B: Emergency laparotomy for splenic haemorrhage
options.C: Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis
options.D: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage at the bedside
options.E: Supine abdominal X-ray and repeat FAST in 1 hour

explanation_correct: The Queensland adult blunt splenic injury guideline states that patients with suspected intra-abdominal injury or bleeding should have a CT abdomen with both arterial and portal venous phases. This grades the injury and shows contrast extravasation (blush). Those findings decide between non-operative management, angioembolisation and surgery in a haemodynamically stable patient.

option_explanations.B: Surgery is for haemodynamic instability or peritonitis. He is stable.
option_explanations.C: Without contrast, CT cannot show active extravasation or vascular injury.
option_explanations.D: DPL is non-specific and largely replaced by FAST and CT in stable patients.
option_explanations.E: Plain films cannot assess solid-organ injury, and a repeat FAST adds little to the first one; it cannot grade the spleen or show a contrast blush.

key_learning_point: In stable blunt abdominal trauma, CT with arterial and portal venous phases grades splenic injury and detects a contrast blush.

subtopic: Tension pneumothorax: immediate decompression
stem: A 35-year-old motorcyclist arrives at an emergency department in Albury, NSW, after a high-speed crash. He is agitated and in severe respiratory distress. Pulse 138/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, SpO2 82% on high-flow oxygen. The trachea is deviated to the left, his neck veins are distended, and the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Urgent chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis
options.B: Large-volume crystalloid bolus for hypotension
options.C: Immediate decompression of the right chest without waiting for imaging
options.D: Rapid sequence intubation before any chest procedure
options.E: Bedside echocardiography to look for tamponade

explanation_correct: This is a clinical diagnosis of tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock. The RCH trauma guideline states that tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock needs urgent pleural decompression by thoracostomy, using anatomical landmarks within the 'triangle of safety', followed by a chest drain. Treatment must not wait for imaging.

option_explanations.A: Waiting for an X-ray in a peri-arrest patient is dangerous.
option_explanations.B: The shock is obstructive, and fluids will not fix it.
option_explanations.D: Positive-pressure ventilation without decompression worsens a tension pneumothorax.
option_explanations.E: The signs point to tension pneumothorax on the right. Decompress without delay.

key_learning_point: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Decompress immediately; do not wait for imaging.

subtopic: Anterior shoulder dislocation: axillary nerve check before reduction
stem: A 22-year-old man fell onto his outstretched arm while skateboarding in Fremantle, WA. His right shoulder is squared off, he holds the arm slightly abducted and externally rotated, and there is a palpable fullness in front of the shoulder. Radial pulse is present.
lead_in: Before reduction, which one of the following is the most important neurological assessment to document?

options.A: Sensation over the first dorsal web space (radial nerve)
options.B: Sensation over the little finger pulp (ulnar nerve)
options.C: Sensation over the regimental badge area (axillary nerve)
options.D: Biceps reflex (C5-6, musculocutaneous nerve)
options.E: Thumb abduction power (median nerve)

explanation_correct: Anterior dislocation can stretch the axillary nerve where it winds around the surgical neck of the humerus. Check and document sensation over the regimental badge area (lateral deltoid) before and after reduction. A review of axillary nerve injury in glenohumeral dislocation warns that preserved sensation there does not rule out motor palsy, so deltoid function must be reassessed after reduction.

option_explanations.A: This is the radial nerve sensory area, which is less often injured in shoulder dislocation.
option_explanations.B: Little finger sensation tests the ulnar nerve, which is rarely injured in anterior shoulder dislocation compared with the axillary nerve.
option_explanations.D: This tests C5–6 and the musculocutaneous nerve. It is not the key check here.
option_explanations.E: Thumb abduction (abductor pollicis brevis) tests the median nerve, which is not at particular risk in anterior dislocation.

key_learning_point: In anterior shoulder dislocation, document regimental badge sensation (axillary nerve) before and after reduction.

subtopic: Suspected ruptured AAA: permissive hypotension and immediate vascular surgery
stem: A 74-year-old man who smokes presents to a regional emergency department in Dubbo, NSW, with sudden severe back and left flank pain and a brief collapse. Pulse 112/min, BP 86/54 mmHg. He is alert and talking. There is a tender pulsatile mass in the epigastrium. Bedside ultrasound shows an infrarenal aorta of 7.2 cm.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Give fluids to keep systolic BP above 120 mmHg before transfer
options.B: Permissive hypotension while he is alert, with immediate referral to vascular surgery for repair
options.C: CT angiogram first, with surgical referral only if rupture is confirmed
options.D: IV labetalol to lower blood pressure
options.E: Admit under general medicine for analgesia and serial ultrasound

explanation_correct: Suspected ruptured AAA in a patient whose cerebration is preserved should be managed with permissive (controlled) hypotension. Avoid aggressive fluids, which dilute clotting factors and can dislodge the clot. Then arrange immediate transfer for endovascular or open repair. The ESVS 2024 guideline recommends permissive hypotension. A CT angiogram is only done if he is stable enough and it will not delay repair.

option_explanations.A: Aggressive fluid resuscitation increases bleeding and mortality.
option_explanations.C: Referral should not wait for CT. Contact the vascular team immediately.
option_explanations.D: Beta-blockers in a hypotensive bleeding patient are harmful. Labetalol is used for dissection, not rupture.
option_explanations.E: A symptomatic aneurysm with collapse and hypotension is a ruptured AAA until proven otherwise; admitting him medically for analgesia and serial ultrasound delays repair of a condition with very high mortality.

key_learning_point: For a ruptured AAA: permissive hypotension while he remains alert, and immediate vascular repair.

subtopic: Epididymo-orchitis in a young man: first-pass urine NAAT
stem: A 23-year-old man presents to a GP in Newcastle, NSW, with three days of right scrotal pain and swelling that began gradually. He has a new female partner and does not use condoms. Temperature 37.8°C. The right epididymis is swollen and tender, the testis lies normally, and the cremasteric reflex is present. There is no urethral discharge.
lead_in: Which one of the following specimens is most important to collect before starting antibiotics?

options.A: First-pass urine for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, plus a midstream urine
options.B: Midstream urine for microscopy and culture only
options.C: Scrotal Doppler ultrasound before any other test
options.D: Serum AFP, beta-hCG and LDH tumour markers
options.E: Two sets of blood cultures and a full blood count

explanation_correct: The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend collecting first-pass urine (for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT) and a midstream urine for epididymo-orchitis, plus a urethral swab for MC&S if there is a discharge. In men under 35, sexually transmitted organisms are the usual cause. Doppler ultrasound is only needed if the diagnosis is uncertain. If torsion is suspected, refer urgently without waiting for an ultrasound.

option_explanations.B: MSU alone misses chlamydia and gonorrhoea, the likely causes at his age.
option_explanations.C: Ultrasound is for diagnostic uncertainty. His presentation is typical.
option_explanations.D: Tumour markers are for a testicular mass, not acute inflammation.
option_explanations.E: He is febrile but not septic or systemically unwell, so blood cultures will not identify the usual sexually transmitted cause; first-pass urine NAAT will.

key_learning_point: In suspected epididymo-orchitis, collect first-pass urine for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT and an MSU before treatment.

subtopic: Perforated peptic ulcer: free subdiaphragmatic gas
stem: A 56-year-old man in Rockhampton, Qld, has had severe epigastric pain for three hours that came on suddenly and is now generalised. He takes ibuprofen regularly for knee osteoarthritis. He is lying very still. Pulse 110/min, BP 108/70 mmHg, temperature 37.6°C. His abdomen is rigid with generalised guarding and absent bowel sounds. Lipase is 90 U/L (<60).
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Acute pancreatitis
options.B: Biliary colic
options.D: Acute mesenteric ischaemia
options.E: Perforated peptic ulcer

explanation_correct: Sudden severe epigastric pain that becomes generalised peritonitis (a board-like abdomen in a patient lying still) in a regular NSAID user strongly suggests a perforated peptic ulcer. The WSES guideline notes that a negative erect X-ray does not exclude perforation, so when there are clear signs of peritonitis CT should be the first imaging test. Lipase can rise slightly with perforation, while pancreatitis needs a lipase at least three times normal.

option_explanations.A: Lipase is only mildly raised (pancreatitis needs more than three times the upper limit) and a board-like abdomen is less typical.
option_explanations.B: Biliary colic does not cause generalised peritonitis.
option_explanations.C: An MI can cause epigastric pain but not a rigid abdomen.
option_explanations.D: Mesenteric ischaemia causes pain out of proportion to examination findings early on. A rigid abdomen from the start fits perforation better.

key_learning_point: Sudden epigastric pain with peritonitis in an NSAID user suggests a perforated peptic ulcer. Mild lipase rises can occur.

subtopic: Peritonsillar abscess: drainage plus antibiotics
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Bundaberg, Qld, with five days of worsening sore throat, now worse on the left. She can barely open her mouth, has a muffled 'hot potato' voice and is drooling. Temperature 38.6°C. Her airway is patent and SpO2 is 98% on room air. The left soft palate is swollen and the uvula is pushed to the right.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and discharge with review in 48 hours
options.B: Emergency surgical tracheostomy to secure the airway
options.C: ENT drainage (needle aspiration or incision) with IV antibiotics
options.D: Immediate (quinsy) tonsillectomy tonight
options.E: IV dexamethasone alone and observe overnight

explanation_correct: Trismus, a hot potato voice and a uvula pushed away from the affected side indicate a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). The PCH WA guideline lists trismus, a unilateral fluctuant swelling extending to the soft palate and uvular deviation as typical. Management is admission under ENT for IV antibiotics with abscess drainage, plus airway assessment and a dose of IV corticosteroid.

option_explanations.A: Oral antibiotics alone do not treat an established abscess, and she is systemically unwell.
option_explanations.B: Her airway is patent with normal saturations; a surgical airway is only for impending obstruction and would be a disproportionate, risky first step.
option_explanations.D: Tonsillectomy in the acute phase is not routine.
option_explanations.E: Steroids may be used alongside other treatment, but they do not replace drainage.

key_learning_point: Quinsy: drain (aspirate or incise) and give IV penicillin-based antibiotics.

subtopic: Post-operative oliguria: prerenal pattern
stem:
A 69-year-old woman is on the surgical ward in Townsville, Qld, on day 1 after an open right hemicolectomy. Her urine output has been 15 mL/h for four hours (weight 70 kg). Her IV fluids were reduced overnight. Pulse 106/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, capillary refill 4 seconds. Her catheter flushes freely.

Investigations:
- Creatinine 128 µmol/L (pre-op 72)
- Urea 14.2 mmol/L
- Urine sodium 9 mmol/L
- Fractional excretion of sodium 0.5%
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her oliguria?

options.A: Acute tubular necrosis
options.B: Blocked urinary catheter
options.D: Post-renal obstruction from urinary retention
options.E: Prerenal acute kidney injury due to hypovolaemia

explanation_correct: She is tachycardic with slow capillary refill, her fluids were cut back, the catheter is patent, and her urine sodium is low (<20 mmol/L) with an FENa below 1%. KDIGO notes that a high urine osmolality with low urine sodium in oliguria shows intact tubular function. In this setting that points to a volume-responsive (prerenal) cause. Give a fluid bolus and reassess, keeping in mind KDIGO's caution that such indices do not mean the AKI is benign.

option_explanations.A: ATN causes a urine sodium above 40 mmol/L and an FENa above 2%.
option_explanations.B: A blocked catheter causes sudden anuria with a distended bladder; hers flushes freely and the low urine sodium shows the kidneys are conserving salt.
option_explanations.C: A ureteric injury would not fit these urine indices or the fluid history.
option_explanations.D: Post-renal obstruction from retention is excluded by a working catheter, and obstruction would not produce a FENa below 1% with a clear hypovolaemic history.

key_learning_point: Post-operative oliguria with low urine sodium and FENa below 1% is prerenal. Give fluid and reassess.

subtopic: Hyperemesis gravidarum: thiamine before glucose
stem:
A 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation is admitted to a hospital in Shepparton, Vic, after two weeks of persistent vomiting. She has kept almost nothing down for five days and has lost 6% of her body weight. Pulse 108/min. Urine ketones 3+.

Investigations:
- Sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L
- Glucose 3.9 mmol/L

IV fluids, potassium replacement and antiemetics are planned.
lead_in: Which one of the following should be given before any glucose-containing IV fluid?

options.A: Intravenous ondansetron
options.B: Oral pyridoxine
options.D: Intravenous thiamine
options.E: Intravenous iron

explanation_correct: After prolonged vomiting and poor intake, thiamine stores are depleted. Glucose can then precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. The NSW Health 2022 guideline recommends IV thiamine 100 mg daily when oral intake is poor or IV glucose is needed. Glucose-containing fluids should only be used after thiamine has been given and hyponatraemia excluded. Rehydration uses 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium as needed.

option_explanations.A: Antiemetics are part of treatment but do not prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
option_explanations.B: Pyridoxine is used for mild nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. It does not replace thiamine.
option_explanations.C: Steroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis.
option_explanations.E: Iron deficiency is common in pregnancy but is not caused or worsened by vomiting over days, and IV iron has no role in preventing Wernicke encephalopathy.

key_learning_point: In hyperemesis with poor intake, give IV thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

subtopic: Suspected ovarian torsion with a large cyst: urgent gynaecology review
stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Mount Gambier, SA, with sudden severe right iliac fossa pain that began four hours ago while she was exercising, with vomiting. Urine β-hCG is negative. She is very tender in the right adnexa. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 7 cm right ovarian cyst, an enlarged right ovary and free fluid.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent gynaecology review for laparoscopy
options.B: Repeat ultrasound in 24 hours
options.D: Discharge with analgesia and outpatient gynaecology review
options.E: Serum CA-125

explanation_correct: An Australian Family Physician review describes ovarian torsion as a gynaecological emergency that needs urgent review. The main risk factor is an ovarian mass larger than 5 cm. Surgery is laparoscopic de-torsion, keeping the ovary where possible, with oophorectomy if it is not viable. Sudden pain with vomiting, a 7 cm cyst and an enlarged ovary make torsion likely, so she should not wait for further tests.

option_explanations.B: Waiting 24 hours for a repeat scan risks irreversible ovarian infarction; torsion is a clinical diagnosis and a normal Doppler does not exclude it.
option_explanations.C: CT delays definitive treatment when torsion is clinically likely.
option_explanations.D: Discharging a woman with probable torsion risks losing the ovary; this is a same-day surgical emergency.
option_explanations.E: CA-125 is non-specific in premenopausal women and plays no part in the emergency management of suspected torsion.

key_learning_point: Suspected ovarian torsion (especially with a mass over 5 cm) is a gynaecological emergency. Get urgent gynaecology review for laparoscopy.

subtopic: Suspected endometriosis: transvaginal ultrasound as a non-invasive diagnostic test
stem: A 22-year-old woman sees her GP in Ipswich, Qld, with severe period pain for four years that is not controlled by regular NSAIDs. She also has pain with deep penetration and painful defecation during her periods. She has had vaginal intercourse and agrees to an internal examination, which shows mild posterior fornix tenderness.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Diagnostic laparoscopy before any imaging
options.B: Serum CA-125
options.D: No investigation; reassure that this is primary dysmenorrhoea
options.E: Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound performed by an experienced sonographer

explanation_correct: RANZCOG's Australian Living Evidence Guideline on endometriosis (endorsed by the RACGP) notes that more cases can now be diagnosed accurately with non-invasive techniques such as transvaginal ultrasound and MRI. Endometriosis no longer always needs surgery for diagnosis, and it can be diagnosed and managed in primary care. A normal scan does not exclude superficial disease. First-line hormonal treatment can still be offered.

option_explanations.A: Surgery is no longer required as the first step in diagnosis.
option_explanations.B: CA-125 is not a diagnostic test for endometriosis.
option_explanations.C: CT is not a recommended test for endometriosis.
option_explanations.D: Her deep dyspareunia and cyclical dyschezia are red flags for endometriosis.

key_learning_point: Suspected endometriosis can be investigated first with an expert transvaginal ultrasound. Laparoscopy is not required first.

subtopic: Missed combined pills in week 1 with unprotected sex: emergency contraception
stem: A 19-year-old woman phones a clinic in Wollongong, NSW. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. She started her new pack three days ago, two days late after the hormone-free week, and has since missed the pills for day 2 and day 3. She had unprotected sex two nights ago. She feels well.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Take a pill now and continue the pack; no other precautions needed
options.B: Stop this pack, use condoms and start a new pack next Sunday
options.C: Take a pill now, use condoms for 7 days, and take emergency contraception
options.D: Take two pills now and use condoms for the next 2 days only
options.E: Do a pregnancy test now and decide about other measures afterwards

explanation_correct: Family Planning NSW advice: a pill more than 24 hours late means taking the most recent missed pill, continuing the pack, and using condoms for 7 days. When more than one pill is missed in the first week of a pack (after the hormone-free interval) and there has been unprotected sex in the previous 5 days, emergency contraception is recommended.

option_explanations.A: With more than one pill missed, she is not protected.
option_explanations.B: Stopping the pack extends the hormone-free interval even further, so ovulation is more likely and she remains unprotected.
option_explanations.D: Extra pills do not restore protection; after a pill is more than 24 hours late, 7 days of continuous active pills (with condoms meanwhile) are needed, and emergency contraception is needed for the recent sex.
option_explanations.E: It is too early for a pregnancy test to be positive, and EC is time-dependent.

key_learning_point: More than one pill missed in week 1 with unprotected sex in the past 5 days: take a pill, use condoms for 7 days, and take EC.

subtopic: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection before 30 weeks
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 27+3 weeks' gestation presents to a tertiary hospital in Randwick, NSW, with regular painful contractions. Her cervix is 6 cm dilated, membranes are intact and fetal monitoring is normal. Birth is expected within hours. Betamethasone has been given.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?

options.A: Oral nifedipine to delay birth by 48 hours
options.B: Intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
options.D: A repeat course of antenatal corticosteroids
options.E: Vaginal progesterone pessaries nightly

explanation_correct: When birth is planned or expected within 24 hours at 24 to under 30 weeks, magnesium sulfate is given for fetal neuroprotection. It reduces the risk of cerebral palsy. This is the indication in the SESLHD/RHW local guideline, which follows the Australian national guideline.

option_explanations.A: She is in advanced labour at 6 cm, so tocolysis is not appropriate.
option_explanations.C: Indomethacin is a tocolytic and is not indicated here.

subtopic: Stress urinary incontinence: supervised pelvic floor muscle training
stem: A 44-year-old woman with three children sees her GP in Albany, WA, with urine leakage when she coughs, laughs or runs. It began after her last birth. She has no urgency or nocturia. Urinalysis is normal and her BMI is 31 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows no significant prolapse.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily
options.B: Referral for a mid-urethral mesh sling
options.D: Vaginal oestrogen cream as the only treatment
options.E: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for 3 months

explanation_correct: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training, for example with a women's health physiotherapist, for at least three months is first-line for stress urinary incontinence. Weight loss and managing cough or constipation help too. Surgery (such as colposuspension or autologous sling) is considered only after conservative treatment fails.

option_explanations.A: Antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin treat urgency (overactive bladder) incontinence; she has pure stress incontinence and they would add side effects without benefit.
option_explanations.B: Mesh slings are not first-line, and their use in Australia has been restricted.
option_explanations.C: Urodynamics are not needed before conservative treatment of uncomplicated stress incontinence.
option_explanations.D: Vaginal oestrogen is not first-line in a premenopausal woman.

key_learning_point: First-line treatment for stress incontinence is supervised pelvic floor training for at least three months.

subtopic: Recurrent miscarriage: antiphospholipid antibody testing
stem: A 33-year-old woman sees a GP in Canberra, ACT, after her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. Each was at 7–9 weeks. She has no other medical history. Her partner is well. Pelvic ultrasound is normal.
lead_in: Which one of the following investigations is most likely to identify a treatable cause?

options.A: Inherited thrombophilia screen (factor V Leiden, protein C and S)
options.B: Antiphospholipid antibodies, repeated at 12 weeks if positive
options.C: Mid-luteal serum progesterone in a non-pregnant cycle
options.D: TORCH serology for chronic maternal infection
options.E: Peripheral blood natural killer cell testing

explanation_correct: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most common acquired thrombophilia and an important treatable cause of recurrent pregnancy loss. The 2024 Australasian RPL guideline lists APS testing as anticardiolipin antibody, lupus anticoagulant and β2-glycoprotein I antibody, using the updated Sydney criteria, which need persistence at least 12 weeks apart. It notes that trials have not shown an association between inherited thrombophilia and RPL, or benefit from LMWH, so inherited thrombophilia screening is not useful.

option_explanations.A: These tests are not recommended for recurrent miscarriage and do not lead to proven treatment.
option_explanations.C: Luteal-phase progesterone does not reliably diagnose luteal insufficiency or predict future miscarriage, and the RPL guideline does not recommend it.
option_explanations.D: Infection is not a cause of recurrent miscarriage.
option_explanations.E: Peripheral NK cell testing does not reflect uterine immunity and there is no proven treatment based on it; the guideline advises against it.

key_learning_point: Recurrent miscarriage: test for antiphospholipid syndrome, confirm at 12 weeks, and treat with aspirin plus heparin in the next pregnancy.

subtopic: Mild croup with stridor at rest: oral dexamethasone
stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to a GP in Warrnambool, Vic, at 9 pm with a barking cough and hoarse voice that started that evening, after two days of a runny nose. He has soft stridor only when he is upset. There is no stridor at rest, no chest wall recession, and he is alert and playing. SpO2 98%.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000, then observe for 4 hours
options.B: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days and review if worse
options.C: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once, then discharge with advice
options.D: Nebulised salbutamol and review in 1 hour
options.E: Lateral neck and chest X-ray before deciding

explanation_correct: RCH guidance for mild croup (stridor only when upset) is a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, or prednisolone 1 mg/kg. Steroids reduce reattendance and shorten symptoms. A barking cough with no stridor at all does not need steroids. Nebulised adrenaline is for severe croup.

option_explanations.A: Nebulised adrenaline is for severe croup (stridor at rest, recession, agitation or lethargy); he only has stridor when upset.
option_explanations.B: Croup is viral (usually parainfluenza); antibiotics have no benefit unless bacterial tracheitis is suspected, which would make him look toxic.
option_explanations.D: Croup is upper airway oedema, not bronchospasm; salbutamol does not help and may increase agitation.
option_explanations.E: Croup is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is only for atypical features (e.g. suspected foreign body) and distressing the child can worsen obstruction.

key_learning_point: Croup with stridor: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. Nebulised adrenaline only for severe croup.

subtopic: Simple febrile seizure: no routine investigations
stem: A 20-month-old girl is brought to an emergency department in Gosford, NSW, after a 2-minute generalised tonic–clonic seizure at home during a fever. She had a runny nose for two days. She is now alert, interactive and back to normal. Temperature 39.0°C. There is no neck stiffness, rash or focal neurological signs, and she is fully immunised.
lead_in: Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate?

options.A: EEG within 48 hours
options.B: Non-contrast CT brain
options.D: FBC, electrolytes, glucose and blood culture
options.E: No routine investigations; look for the source of the fever clinically

explanation_correct: This is a simple febrile seizure. RCH guidelines state that investigations are low yield and not routinely needed. Assess for the focus of the fever clinically. Investigations are targeted only for atypical or complex seizures or a suspected serious infection.

option_explanations.A: An EEG does not predict recurrence or epilepsy after a simple febrile seizure.
option_explanations.B: Neuroimaging is for focal seizures, focal signs, a persistently reduced conscious state or suspected trauma; she is back to normal.
option_explanations.C: She is alert with no meningism, so LP is not indicated.
option_explanations.D: Routine bloods do not change management in a well child after a simple febrile seizure; they are only targeted if the child looks unwell or the seizure was complex.

key_learning_point: Simple febrile seizure in a well child: no routine tests; find the fever source clinically.

subtopic: First presentation of nephrotic syndrome: prednisolone regimen
stem: A 4-year-old boy in Hobart, Tas, has had puffy eyes for one week and now has swollen legs. BP is normal. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein with no blood. Serum albumin is 15 g/L, creatinine is normal and complement is normal. A diagnosis of likely steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome is made. He weighs 18 kg (body surface area 0.74 m²).
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: Renal biopsy before starting any treatment
options.B: IV 20% albumin with furosemide, without steroids
options.D: Prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m2 alternate days for 4 weeks
options.E: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 7 days, then stop if urine is protein-free

explanation_correct: RCH guidelines for a first presentation recommend prednisolone 60 mg/m² (or 2 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg) daily for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m² (or 1.5 mg/kg, maximum 40 mg) on alternate days for 4 weeks. A renal biopsy is not routinely needed in typical cases at this age.

option_explanations.A: A typical presentation at this age does not need a biopsy.
option_explanations.B: Albumin with furosemide treats symptomatic oedema or hypovolaemia only; it does not induce remission, which needs corticosteroids.
option_explanations.C: Cyclophosphamide is for frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent disease.
option_explanations.E: This dose and duration are too low and too short; short courses are associated with more relapses than the standard 8-week regimen.

key_learning_point: First-episode nephrotic syndrome: prednisolone 60 mg/m² daily for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m² alternate days for 4 weeks.

subtopic: Prolonged jaundice: conjugated bilirubin and biliary atresia
stem:
A 4-week-old breastfed boy is brought to a GP in Kalgoorlie, WA, because he is still jaundiced. He is feeding well and gaining weight. His mother thinks his stools have been pale for a week. His urine is dark yellow.

Investigations:
- Total bilirubin 160 µmol/L
- Conjugated bilirubin 70 µmol/L
- Liver ultrasound: normal liver; gallbladder seen
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure: this is breast milk jaundice; review at 8 weeks
options.B: Same-day discussion and referral to paediatric gastroenterology
options.D: Stop breastfeeding for 48 hours, then recheck
options.E: Home phototherapy

explanation_correct: A conjugated bilirubin above 20 µmol/L (or more than 20% of the total) is abnormal, and with pale stools it suggests biliary atresia until proven otherwise. RCH guidelines state that a normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia. Urgent referral matters because outcomes of Kasai surgery are better when it is done early.

option_explanations.A: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated; a conjugated bilirubin of 70 µmol/L (over 20% of total) with pale stools is pathological.
option_explanations.C: Waiting 2 weeks delays the diagnosis of biliary atresia; Kasai outcomes are best before about 60 days of age.
option_explanations.D: Interrupting breastfeeding is not indicated for conjugated jaundice and does not address the cholestasis.
option_explanations.E: Phototherapy treats unconjugated bilirubin only and can cause bronze baby syndrome in cholestasis.

key_learning_point: Prolonged jaundice with conjugated bilirubin above 20 µmol/L or pale stools needs urgent gastroenterology referral. A normal US does not exclude biliary atresia.

subtopic: Limping febrile child: septic arthritis vs transient synovitis
stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to an emergency department in Geraldton, WA, with one day of refusing to walk on her right leg. Temperature 38.9°C. She holds her hip flexed and externally rotated and resists all movement.

Investigations:
- WCC 17.8 × 10⁹/L
- CRP 96 mg/L
- ESR 55 mm/h
- Hip ultrasound: effusion
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and plan?

options.A: Transient synovitis; oral NSAIDs and review in 48 hours
options.B: Possible osteomyelitis; non-urgent MRI next week
options.C: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis; urgent frog-leg X-rays
options.D: Likely septic arthritis; urgent orthopaedic aspiration and washout
options.E: Perthes disease; orthopaedic outpatient referral

explanation_correct: RCH guidelines describe septic arthritis as an orthopaedic emergency. An effusion on ultrasound does not distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis, but fever, refusal to bear weight and raised WCC, CRP and ESR all point to infection. She needs urgent orthopaedic referral for aspiration and washout, with IV antibiotics given after cultures are taken.

option_explanations.A: Her fever and inflammatory markers argue strongly against transient synovitis.
option_explanations.B: Septic arthritis is an orthopaedic emergency; MRI may help if osteomyelitis is suspected, but it must not delay aspiration and washout.
option_explanations.C: Slipped epiphysis is unlikely at age 5 and does not cause fever.
option_explanations.E: Perthes disease causes an insidious limp in an afebrile child with normal inflammatory markers; it does not cause fever or a CRP of 96.

key_learning_point: A febrile child who won't bear weight and has raised markers and an effusion has septic arthritis until proven otherwise; it is an orthopaedic emergency.

subtopic: Anaphylaxis with wheeze in an asthmatic child: adrenaline first
stem: A 9-year-old boy with asthma eats a muesli bar containing peanut at school camp near Kiama, NSW. Within 10 minutes he has hives, lip swelling, a hoarse voice, wheeze and difficulty breathing. A nurse is present with an adrenaline autoinjector, salbutamol and oral antihistamine.
lead_in: Which one of the following should be given first?

options.A: Salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer
options.B: Oral cetirizine 10 mg
options.D: IM adrenaline into the outer thigh
options.E: Subcutaneous adrenaline into the arm

explanation_correct: He has anaphylaxis with respiratory involvement. RCH guidelines say IM adrenaline must be given first, and in a child with asthma, adrenaline comes before any asthma medicine. Antihistamines and steroids should not be given as treatment of anaphylaxis. Adrenaline should not be given subcutaneously.

option_explanations.A: Salbutamol treats bronchospasm but not the airway oedema or circulatory effects of anaphylaxis; in a child with asthma, adrenaline is given first.
option_explanations.B: Antihistamines are not a treatment for anaphylaxis.
option_explanations.C: Steroids are not a treatment for anaphylaxis.
option_explanations.E: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less reliable; IM into the anterolateral thigh gives faster peak levels.

key_learning_point: Anaphylaxis in a child with asthma: IM adrenaline first, before salbutamol.

subtopic: Panic disorder: CBT first-line
stem: A 29-year-old man sees his GP in Perth, WA, after three emergency department visits in four months with sudden episodes of palpitations, chest tightness, tingling and fear of dying, each lasting about 15 minutes. ECG, troponin, TSH and full blood count were normal each time. He now avoids trains in case an attack happens. He drinks little alcohol and uses no drugs.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: Regular alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily
options.B: Propranolol 10 mg as needed for attacks
options.D: CBT with interoceptive and in-vivo exposure
options.E: Low-dose quetiapine at night

explanation_correct: This is panic disorder with avoidance. The Australian comorbidity guidelines, citing the RANZCP guideline, recommend 8–12 sessions of face-to-face or guided digital CBT as first-line treatment for panic disorder. Medication can be used as an alternative or addition for moderate to severe illness or when CBT does not help enough. Benzodiazepines are not recommended for ongoing treatment.

option_explanations.A: Benzodiazepines carry a risk of dependence and are not recommended.
option_explanations.B: Propranolol is not effective for panic disorder.
option_explanations.C: Three normal ED work-ups and a typical history make a cardiac arrhythmia unlikely; further cardiac testing reinforces illness beliefs and delays effective treatment.
option_explanations.E: Antipsychotics are not recommended for panic disorder and carry metabolic and other harms.

key_learning_point: First-line treatment for panic disorder is CBT with exposure, with an SSRI as an alternative or addition. Avoid benzodiazepines.

subtopic: Recognising treatment-resistant schizophrenia
stem: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia is reviewed by a community mental health team in Footscray, Vic. He still has persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations that stop him working. He had 6 weeks of risperidone, with adherence confirmed because it was given as a long-acting injection at a therapeutic dose, and then 8 weeks of olanzapine 20 mg daily, with adherence confirmed by plasma levels. Neither helped. He does not use substances, and organic causes have been excluded.
lead_in: Which one of the following best describes his illness, and what does it imply?

options.A: Pseudo-resistance from non-adherence
options.B: Schizoaffective disorder needing a mood stabiliser
options.C: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia; a clozapine trial should be started promptly
options.D: Ultra-treatment-resistant schizophrenia needing ECT
options.E: Inadequate trial; continue olanzapine for another 6 months

explanation_correct: He has had two adequate antipsychotic trials, with confirmed adherence and adequate dose and duration, and still has significant symptoms. This meets the definition of treatment-resistant schizophrenia. The RANZCP-endorsed INTEGRATE guidelines say that if two adequate trials fail, a clozapine trial should be started promptly, aiming for plasma levels of 350–500 ng/mL.

option_explanations.A: Pseudo-resistance means apparent non-response due to non-adherence or inadequate dose; his adherence was confirmed by LAI administration and plasma levels.
option_explanations.B: Schizoaffective disorder needs mood episodes for a substantial part of the illness; he has no prominent mood symptoms.
option_explanations.D: That term applies only after clozapine has failed.
option_explanations.E: Both trials were adequate in dose and duration.

key_learning_point: Two adequate antipsychotic trials that have failed define treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Start clozapine promptly.

subtopic: Functional neurological disorder: positive Hoover sign
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to a hospital in Logan, Qld, with sudden weakness of her right leg that began after a stressful week at work. She can barely lift her right leg off the bed. When she is asked to flex her left hip against resistance, strong involuntary extension of the right hip is felt. Reflexes are symmetrical, plantar responses are flexor and sensation is normal. MRI of the brain and spine is normal.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Malingering for secondary gain
options.B: Positive Hoover sign, consistent with functional weakness
options.D: Acute L5 lumbar radiculopathy
options.E: Lacunar stroke of the internal capsule

explanation_correct: A positive Hoover sign means hip extension is weak when tested directly but returns to normal during contralateral hip flexion. It is a positive clinical sign of functional weakness. FND is diagnosed on positive features, not by exclusion alone. It is not feigning. Treatment involves explaining the diagnosis clearly, then physiotherapy and psychological therapy.

option_explanations.A: Malingering is deliberate feigning for gain; functional neurological disorder is not intentional, and a positive Hoover sign does not distinguish intent.
option_explanations.C: MRI is normal and there are no upper motor neuron signs.
option_explanations.D: Radiculopathy causes weakness in a myotomal pattern with dermatomal sensory change and reduced reflexes, and the weakness does not resolve with contralateral hip flexion.
option_explanations.E: A lacunar stroke gives upper motor neurone signs (hyperreflexia, extensor plantar) and the MRI is normal; strength would not return during contralateral hip flexion.

key_learning_point: Hoover sign is a positive sign of functional weakness. FND is diagnosed on positive features, and it is not feigning.

subtopic: Bulimia nervosa: check potassium
stem: A 20-year-old university student in Newcastle, NSW, tells her GP she binge-eats several times a week and then makes herself vomit. Her BMI is 22 kg/m². She has bilateral parotid swelling and calluses on the backs of her fingers. She feels lightheaded at times.
lead_in: Which one of the following investigations is most important at this visit?

options.A: Serum amylase and lipase
options.B: DEXA bone density scan
options.D: Non-contrast CT brain
options.E: Serum electrolytes and an ECG

explanation_correct: Self-induced vomiting causes hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, which can lead to arrhythmias. Australian Prescriber states that a physical examination, FBC, urea and electrolytes (including phosphate) and an ECG are mandatory to assess the physical complications of purging. Hypokalaemia may even be the first clue to an eating disorder. Psychological treatment is eating-disorder-focused CBT.

option_explanations.A: Amylase may be raised from the parotid glands but does not change management.
option_explanations.B: Low bone density is a complication of prolonged low weight (anorexia nervosa); her BMI is normal and DEXA does not address the immediate danger.
option_explanations.C: Thyroid disease does not explain self-induced vomiting and is not the urgent risk; hypokalaemia from purging is.
option_explanations.D: She has no neurological features; lightheadedness is explained by dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.

key_learning_point: In bulimia with purging, check potassium (hypokalaemic alkalosis can cause arrhythmia).

subtopic: New agitation in dementia: assess for delirium, pain and unmet needs first
stem: An 84-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease in a residential aged care facility in Launceston, Tas, has become agitated in the late afternoons over the past five days, calling out and pacing. She communicates little verbally. Staff ask the GP for 'something to settle her'. Her regular medicines have not changed.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate first step in assessment?

options.A: Start regular low-dose risperidone 0.25 mg
options.B: Arrange a non-contrast CT brain
options.C: Assess for delirium, pain and unmet needs
options.D: Repeat cognitive testing with the MMSE
options.E: Arrange an EEG to exclude seizures

explanation_correct: The NSW Health BPSD handbook asks first whether delirium is present and whether the person could be in pain, need the toilet, or have other unmet basic needs. Delirium causes and pain must be treated before behaviour is attributed to dementia. A structured pain tool (for example, the Abbey Pain Scale), examination, bowel and bladder review and a look for infection are first steps. Non-pharmacological strategies come before medication.

option_explanations.A: Medication is not the first step, and the behaviour has not yet been assessed for a cause.
option_explanations.B: CT is not routine for new agitation without focal signs or a fall.
option_explanations.D: Repeat testing does not identify the cause of the acute change.
option_explanations.E: EEG is not a first-line test for new agitation in dementia; common causes such as pain, infection, constipation and retention must be looked for first.

key_learning_point: New BPSD: look for delirium, pain and unmet needs first.

subtopic: Long-term benzodiazepine use: gradual taper
stem: A 58-year-old man in Toowoomba, Qld, has taken oxazepam 30 mg three times daily for six years. It was first prescribed after a bereavement. He would now like to stop. He has no history of seizures and does not drink alcohol.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Switch to equivalent diazepam and taper over months
options.B: Stop oxazepam today with a 2-week PRN supply
options.D: Switch to zolpidem at night, then stop oxazepam
options.E: Admit for flumazenil-assisted withdrawal

explanation_correct: Stopping benzodiazepines abruptly after long-term use risks withdrawal seizures. Australian Prescriber advises a gradual dose reduction over weeks to months, often after switching to diazepam because its long half-life gives a smoother taper.

option_explanations.B: Abrupt cessation after 6 years of high-dose use risks severe withdrawal including seizures and delirium.
option_explanations.C: Halving the dose each week would stop the drug within a month, far faster than the weeks-to-months taper recommended for long-term use.
option_explanations.D: This just substitutes another dependence-causing drug.
option_explanations.E: Flumazenil precipitates acute withdrawal and seizures in dependent patients; it has no role in planned withdrawal.

key_learning_point: Stop long-term benzodiazepines with a slow taper, often after switching to diazepam.

subtopic: Positive likelihood ratio from sensitivity and specificity
stem: A new point-of-care test for deep vein thrombosis has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 70% compared with compression ultrasound.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the positive likelihood ratio of this test?
explanation_correct: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity) = 0.90 ÷ 0.30 = 3.0. A positive result triples the pre-test odds.

option_explanations.A: This is sensitivity divided by specificity (0.9 / 0.7), which is not a likelihood ratio; the denominator for LR+ is the false-positive rate (1 - specificity).
option_explanations.C: This is the negative likelihood ratio, (1 - sensitivity) / specificity = 0.1 / 0.7.
option_explanations.D: This is 1 ÷ LR+, the reciprocal, which is not a likelihood ratio.
option_explanations.E: This is sensitivity × specificity, which has no diagnostic meaning.

key_learning_point: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity).
