subtopic: Recall bias in a case–control study
stem: A case–control study in Victoria compares mothers of infants born with a congenital heart defect with mothers of healthy infants. All are asked months after the birth about over-the-counter medicines they took in early pregnancy. Case mothers report more medicine use.
lead_in: Which one of the following biases is most likely to explain part of this association?

options.A: Lead-time bias
options.B: Healthy worker effect
options.D: Length-time bias
options.E: Recall bias

explanation_correct: Mothers of affected infants are more likely to search their memories and report exposures. This differential misclassification of exposure is recall bias, and it is typical of case–control studies that rely on self-report.

option_explanations.A: Lead-time bias is an apparent survival gain from diagnosing disease earlier by screening; this is a case-control study of exposure, not survival.
option_explanations.B: The healthy worker effect is lower morbidity in employed cohorts compared with the general population; no occupational cohort is involved.
option_explanations.C: Loss to follow-up affects cohort studies and trials; a case-control study recruits on outcome and has no follow-up period.
option_explanations.D: Length-time bias belongs to screening studies.

key_learning_point: Self-reported past exposures in case–control studies are prone to recall bias.

subtopic: Relative risk calculation from a cohort
stem: In a cohort of 2,000 Queensland farm workers followed for 5 years, 1,000 worked regularly with livestock and 1,000 did not. Leptospirosis was diagnosed in 20 livestock workers and 5 non-livestock workers.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the relative risk of leptospirosis for livestock work?

option_explanations.A: This is the risk difference (2.0% - 0.5% = 1.5%), an absolute measure, not the relative risk.
option_explanations.B: This is the inverse ratio (unexposed over exposed, 0.005 / 0.02).
option_explanations.C: This is the difference in case counts (20 - 5), which ignores the denominators.
option_explanations.D: This is the risk in the exposed (20/1000), not the ratio.

key_learning_point: RR = risk in the exposed ÷ risk in the unexposed.

subtopic: Suspected measles: notify the public health unit on clinical suspicion
stem: A 24-year-old unvaccinated man returned to Sydney from Southeast Asia nine days ago. He sees a GP with three days of fever, cough, conjunctivitis and coryza, and since this morning a maculopapular rash spreading from his face. The GP isolates him in a separate room. Serology and PCR swabs are collected.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next action regarding public health?

options.A: Wait for PCR confirmation before notifying public health
options.B: Notify the public health unit by phone now, before results
options.C: Notify public health only if the patient consents to it
options.D: Contact his workplace directly to warn his colleagues
options.E: Notify by routine written form once the rash has resolved

explanation_correct: The NSW Health measles control guideline asks emergency departments and medical practitioners to report suspected cases to the local public health unit promptly, and to seek laboratory confirmation in all suspected cases. Early notification of a suspected case allows contact tracing and post-exposure prophylaxis within the time when it works. Cases should stay home until 4 days after rash onset.

option_explanations.A: Notification should happen on clinical suspicion.
option_explanations.C: Notification of notifiable conditions does not need the patient's consent.
option_explanations.D: Contact tracing is coordinated by the public health unit.
option_explanations.E: Measles is notified urgently by telephone on clinical suspicion so contacts can receive MMR within 72 hours or immunoglobulin within 6 days; delayed written notification misses that window.

key_learning_point: Suspected measles: isolate, test and notify the public health unit promptly on clinical suspicion.

subtopic: BreastScreen eligibility: symptomatic woman needs diagnostic pathway
stem: A 46-year-old woman sees her GP in Darwin, NT, with a new 2 cm firm lump in her left breast that she noticed three weeks ago. She asks whether she should book a free BreastScreen mammogram.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Refer for diagnostic imaging and assessment via her GP, not BreastScreen
options.B: Book BreastScreen, as women aged 40-49 may attend free
options.C: Wait for her BreastScreen invitation at age 50
options.D: Review the lump after her next period, then decide
options.E: Refer for BRCA genetic testing before any imaging

explanation_correct: BreastScreen Australia invites women aged 50–74 every 2 years, and women aged 40–49 or 75 and over may book if they have no symptoms. Women with symptoms should see their doctor for diagnostic imaging (the triple test).

option_explanations.B: She has symptoms, so screening is not the right pathway.
option_explanations.C: A new breast lump needs diagnostic assessment now, at any age; screening invitations are for women without symptoms.
option_explanations.D: Re-examining after a period is reasonable only for a premenopausal woman with a vague, cyclical thickening; a discrete 2 cm lump present for 3 weeks needs the triple test now.
option_explanations.E: Genetic testing is for women with a strong family history or a diagnosed cancer meeting criteria; it does not assess this lump.

key_learning_point: BreastScreen is for women without symptoms. A breast lump needs the diagnostic triple-test pathway.

subtopic: Q fever vaccination: pre-vaccination screening
stem: A 23-year-old woman starting work at an abattoir in Wagga Wagga, NSW, attends for Q fever vaccination. Pre-vaccination testing shows a negative Q fever antibody serology, and the skin test, read 7 days later, is positive (induration 6 mm).
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and action?

options.A: She is sensitised and should not be vaccinated
options.B: Vaccinate because serology is negative
options.C: Repeat the skin test in 1 week
options.D: Vaccinate with a half dose
options.E: Treat with doxycycline then vaccinate

explanation_correct: The Australian Immunisation Handbook states that a positive result on either serology or skin test means the person is sensitised and must not be vaccinated, because of the risk of severe local reactions. Vaccination goes ahead only if both tests are negative.

option_explanations.B: A positive skin test still means she is sensitised.
option_explanations.C: Repeating the skin test does not change the result; a positive test means prior sensitisation, and a repeat test itself risks a local reaction.
option_explanations.D: There is no reduced-dose Q fever vaccine regimen; sensitised people must not be vaccinated at all.
option_explanations.E: A positive skin test reflects past exposure (immunity), not active infection, so antibiotics are not indicated and vaccination remains contraindicated.

key_learning_point: Q fever: vaccinate only if both serology and skin test are negative.
